questions.question: The Pollaczek-Khinchine formula $\mathbb{E}[W]=\frac{\lambda\,\mathbb{E}[S^2]}{2(1-\rho)}$ for the mean waiting time in queue holds under which set of assumptions, with $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$?
options: General i.i.d. interarrival times with rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. exponential service times, one server, $\rho<1$.
Poisson arrivals, i.i.d. general service times with finite mean $\mathbb{E}[S]$ only, one server, $\rho<1$.
Poisson arrivals, i.i.d. general service times with $\mathbb{E}[S^2]<\infty$, one server in order of arrival, $\rho<1$.
Poisson arrivals, i.i.d. services with finite variance, a single server, and any load up to full use, $\rho\le1$.

questions.question: In the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula $\mathbb{E}[W]=\frac{\lambda\,\mathbb{E}[S^2]}{2(1-\rho)}=\frac{1+C_s^2}{2}\,\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\,\mathbb{E}[S]$ for an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$ with $\mathbb{E}[S^2]<\infty$, one server in arrival order, $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$), what does $\mathbb{E}[W]$ measure?
options: The mean time a job spends in the queue, from its arrival until its own service starts.
The mean time a job spends in the system, from its arrival until its own service ends.
The long-run mean number of jobs that are waiting in the queue, not counting the job in service.
The mean remaining service time of the job in service, as seen by an arriving job.

questions.question: Two queues are both an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$ with $\mathbb{E}[S^2]<\infty$, one server in arrival order, $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$). They have the same $\lambda$, the same $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and the same finite $\operatorname{Var}(S)$, but different service-time distributions. How do their mean waiting times $\mathbb{E}[W]$ compare?
options: The queue whose service distribution has the heavier right tail has the larger $\mathbb{E}[W]$, since rare long jobs block the server.
They cannot be compared from these data, because $\mathbb{E}[W]$ also depends on the third moment $\mathbb{E}[S^3]$.
They are equal only if both services are exponential, because the formula is exact only in the M/M/1 case $C_s^2=1$.
They are equal, because the formula depends on the service time only through $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and $\mathbb{E}[S^2]$.

questions.question: Queues A and B are both an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$ with $\mathbb{E}[S^2]<\infty$, one server in arrival order, $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$). They have the same $\rho$ and the same $C_s^2$, but B's mean service time is twice A's, $\mathbb{E}[S_B]=2\,\mathbb{E}[S_A]$, so $\lambda_B=\lambda_A/2$. What is $\mathbb{E}[W_B]/\mathbb{E}[W_A]$?
options: $1$, because the waiting time depends only on the load $\rho$ and on the variability $C_s^2$.
$2$, because only the time-scale factor $\mathbb{E}[S]$ differs between the two queues.
$4$, because $\mathbb{E}[S^2]$ is four times as large in queue B as in queue A.
$\tfrac{1}{2}$, because jobs arrive at half the rate, so each job meets half as many others.

questions.question: For an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$ with $\mathbb{E}[S^2]<\infty$, one server in arrival order, $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$), keep $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and $C_s^2$ fixed and raise $\lambda$ so that $\rho$ increases towards $1$. How does $\mathbb{E}[W]$ behave according to the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula?
options: It grows in proportion to $\rho$, so equal steps in the load add equal amounts of waiting time.
It levels off at a finite value, because only one job at a time can be in service.
It grows faster and faster and without bound, because of the factor $\rho/(1-\rho)$.
It grows without bound only when $C_s^2>0$; with deterministic services it stays bounded.

questions.question: In an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$, one server in arrival order, load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$), jobs arrive at $\lambda=0.2$ per minute and service times have $\mathbb{E}[S]=2$ minutes and $\mathbb{E}[S^2]=10$ minutes$^2$. What is the mean waiting time in queue $\mathbb{E}[W]=\frac{\lambda\,\mathbb{E}[S^2]}{2(1-\rho)}$?
options: About $3.33$ minutes
About $1.67$ minutes
$1.00$ minute
About $0.67$ minute

questions.question: A workstation is an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$, one server in arrival order, load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$). Jobs arrive at $12$ per working day of $8$ hours, the mean service time is $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.5$ hour and $C_s^2=1/3$. What is $\mathbb{E}[W]=\frac{1+C_s^2}{2}\,\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\,\mathbb{E}[S]$ in hours?
options: $1.5$ hours
$0.25$ hour
About $1.33$ hours
$1$ hour

questions.question: A printer handles jobs as an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$, one server in arrival order, load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$). Every job prints in exactly $2$ minutes and jobs arrive at $\lambda=0.4$ per minute. On average, how long does a job wait before its printing starts?
options: $4$ minutes
$8$ minutes
$0$ minutes
$1$ minute

questions.question: For an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$, one server in arrival order, load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$) with $\lambda=2$ per hour and $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.25$ hour, the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula gives $\mathbb{E}[W]=0.6$ hour. What is the mean number of jobs in the system, $\mathbb{E}[L]$?
options: $1.2$ jobs
$0.85$ jobs
$1.7$ jobs
$1.45$ jobs

questions.question: In an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$, one server in arrival order, load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$), service times are exponential with mean $3$ minutes and jobs arrive at $\lambda=0.2$ per minute. Using $\mathbb{E}[W]=\frac{1+C_s^2}{2}\,\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\,\mathbb{E}[S]$, what is $\mathbb{E}[W]$?
options: $22.5$ minutes
$4.5$ minutes
$9$ minutes
$1.5$ minutes

questions.question: In an M/G/1 queue with arrival rate $\lambda$ and load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$, PASTA gives $\mathbb{E}[W]=\mathbb{E}[S_r]+\mathbb{E}[Q]\,\mathbb{E}[S]$, with $S_r$ the remaining service time of the job in service, and Little's law gives $\mathbb{E}[Q]=\lambda\mathbb{E}[W]$. What follows for $\mathbb{E}[W]$?
options: $\mathbb{E}[W]=\mathbb{E}[S_r](1+\rho)$, since the jobs in queue add one extra round of load $\rho$.
$\mathbb{E}[W]=\mathbb{E}[S_r]/(1-\lambda)$, since $\lambda\mathbb{E}[W]$ jobs are in queue on average.
$\mathbb{E}[W]=\mathbb{E}[S_r]/(1-\rho)$, valid for every load $\rho\ne1$ of the server.
$\mathbb{E}[W]=\mathbb{E}[S_r]/(1-\rho)$, valid when $\rho<1$ so that the solution is positive and finite.

questions.question: In an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$ with $\mathbb{E}[S^2]<\infty$, one server in arrival order, $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$), $\mathbb{E}[W]=\mathbb{E}[S_r]/(1-\rho)$, where $\mathbb{E}[S_r]$ is the mean remaining service time an arrival finds ($0$ if the server is idle). Which statement correctly gives and explains $\mathbb{E}[S_r]$?
options: $\mathbb{E}[S_r]=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S^2]/2$, because an arrival is more likely to land in a long service than in a short one.
$\mathbb{E}[S_r]=\rho\,\mathbb{E}[S]/2$, because a busy server has on average half a mean service time left.
$\mathbb{E}[S_r]=\rho\,\mathbb{E}[S]$, because Poisson arrivals are memoryless, so the service in progress restarts.
$\mathbb{E}[S_r]=\lambda\operatorname{Var}(S)/2$, because only the spread of $S$ around its mean creates remaining work.

questions.question: A machine is an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, one server, $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$) with exponential services, $C_s^2=1$. It is replaced by one with deterministic services, $C_s^2=0$, and the same $\lambda$ and $\mathbb{E}[S]$. What happens to $\rho$ and to the mean queue length $\mathbb{E}[Q]$?
options: Both $\rho$ and $\mathbb{E}[Q]$ are halved, because the variability factor halves.
$\rho$ stays the same and $\mathbb{E}[Q]$ is halved, because only $\mathbb{E}[W]$ changes.
Both $\rho$ and $\mathbb{E}[Q]$ stay the same, because both depend only on $\lambda$ and $\mathbb{E}[S]$.
$\rho$ is halved and $\mathbb{E}[Q]$ stays the same, because regular jobs occupy the server less.

questions.question: In an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$, one server in arrival order, load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$), service times are uniform on $[0,3]$ hours, $S\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,3)$, and jobs arrive at $\lambda=0.25$ per hour. What is the mean sojourn time $\mathbb{E}[J]$?
options: $0.6$ hour
$1.95$ hours
$2.1$ hours
$2.4$ hours

questions.question: Customers at a desk form an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$, one server in arrival order, load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$) with arrival rate $\lambda=0.25$ per minute. A service takes $1$ minute or $3$ minutes, each with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, independently of everything else. Compute $\mathbb{E}[W]$, the mean time in queue.
options: About $2.33$ minutes
$0.25$ minute
$2$ minutes
$1.25$ minutes

questions.question: A workstation is an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$, one server in arrival order, load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$) with $\lambda=0.5$ per hour, $\mathbb{E}[S]=1.6$ hours and $C_s^2=0.5$, so $\mathbb{E}[W]=4.8$ hours. Faster tooling cuts $\mathbb{E}[S]$ to $1.2$ hours, with $\lambda$ and $C_s^2$ unchanged. What is the new $\mathbb{E}[W]$?
options: $1.35$ hours
$3.6$ hours
$2.7$ hours
$1.8$ hours

questions.question: The derivation of the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula uses PASTA, Little's law $\mathbb{E}[Q]=\lambda\mathbb{E}[W]$ and the time-average remaining service time $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S^2]/2$. If the Poisson arrivals are replaced by general i.i.d. interarrival times with rate $\lambda$ and $\rho<1$, which step can fail?
options: Little's law $\mathbb{E}[Q]=\lambda\mathbb{E}[W]$, because it needs Poisson arrivals to hold.
The step where an arriving job sees the time-average queue length and remaining service time.
The time-average remaining service time $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S^2]/2$, because its proof needs Poisson arrivals.
The load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ as the long-run fraction of time the server is busy.

questions.question: In a single-server queue with Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, served in order of arrival, the i.i.d. service times $S$ have finite mean with $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]=0.5$ but infinite second moment, $\mathbb{E}[S^2]=\infty$. What can be said about the mean waiting time $\mathbb{E}[W]$?
options: It is finite and equals $\rho\,\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)$, because with $\rho<1$ only the mean service time matters.
It is finite but cannot be computed, because $C_s^2$ is undefined, while the queue remains stable.
It is infinite because the queue is unstable: an infinite second moment pushes the load above $1$.
It is infinite although the queue is stable, because arrivals meet an infinite mean remaining service time.

questions.question: A counter is an M/G/1 queue (Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service times $S$, one server in arrival order, load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$) with $\lambda=0.9$ per minute, $\mathbb{E}[S]=1$ minute and $C_s^2=1$, so $\mathbb{E}[W]=9$ minutes. Keeping $\mathbb{E}[S]=1$ minute, which plan gives $\mathbb{E}[W]$ of at most $3$ minutes?
options: Make services deterministic, $C_s^2=0$, and keep $\lambda=0.9$ per minute.
Halve the variability to $C_s^2=0.5$ and lower $\lambda$ to $0.85$ per minute.
Keep $C_s^2=1$ and lower $\lambda$ to $0.75$ per minute.
Make services deterministic, $C_s^2=0$, and lower $\lambda$ to $0.88$ per minute.

questions.question: Jobs arrive as a Poisson process at $\lambda=0.8$ per minute at a single machine, served in order of arrival. Machine A has mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]=1$ minute with standard deviation $0.5$ minute; machine B has $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.8$ minute with standard deviation $1.6$ minutes. Which machine gives the smaller mean waiting time $\mathbb{E}[W]$, and what are the two values?
options: Machine A: $2.50$ minutes, against about $3.56$ minutes for B.
Machine B: about $2.13$ minutes, against $3.00$ minutes for A.
Machine B: about $1.42$ minutes, against $4.00$ minutes for A.
Machine A: $0.50$ minute, against about $2.84$ minutes for B.
